title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of training-data sourcing. Suno admitted that its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the scraped sources. No licensing agreements with rights holders were in place before deployment. The system was then made publicly available in a form that could reproduce recognizable sections of specific copyrighted recordings, as demonstrated when record labels used targeted prompts to generate outputs closely mimicking works by named artists across dozens of attempts.

This is a case of a generative model deployed at scale without the rights clearances that the underlying data required. The failure point was in the data-collection and legal-review stage, before any model was trained, not in the inference pipeline itself. A rights-clearance process, or even a filtering step to exclude commercially distributed recordings, would have been the intervention point. Instead the system went to market, and the gap between what was ingested and what was licensed only became visible through litigation and external reporting.

What is not established: the lawsuits and class actions are allegations, not verdicts, and the German court ruling against Suno and the various settlements with Warner and Universal are the only resolved legal outcomes described in the reporting. Whether Suno or Udio acted with deliberate intent to infringe, as distinct from making a legal judgment about fair use that courts have since rejected in some jurisdictions, is not proven by the filings alone.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim that these services not only used unauthorized training data but also generate songs that directly reproduce sections of famous recordings. The record labels submitted thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were scraped, including music from artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To build their case, the record labels demonstrated that they could recreate versions of famous songs by using targeted prompts describing specific decades, genres, and artist styles. For example, they generated a song mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" in 29 different outputs and created near-identical versions of Green Day's "American Idiot" and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits, filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, argue that the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and falsely claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use.
